topic: What genes make us uniquely human?
topic_context: The project investigates human-lineage genetic differences, including duplicated genes and regulatory sequence changes, that may contribute to human-specific brain development.
scientific_reframing: Which human-lineage genetic changes causally alter a defined early cortical developmental transition, through which molecular pathway, and under what evidence conditions can that effect be generalized beyond one cell line or organoid protocol?

selected_primary_direction.name: CortexSwitch
selected_primary_direction.title: Reciprocal Multiplex Causal Mapping of Human-Lineage Cortical Developmental Modules
candidate_axes: state-active human accelerated or human-specific three-dimensional regulatory candidates
selected_primary_direction.central_hypothesis: A compact, evidence-qualified combination of human-lineage coding and regulatory changes can shift a conserved progenitor-to-neuron transition through a measurable molecular program, with support requiring reciprocal, line-aware, organoid-fidelity-qualified evidence.
primary_endpoints: basal radial glia abundance and persistence
candidate-linked transcriptional and chromatin mediator states
falsification_conditions: No reciprocal sign-consistent effect across qualified independent lines.
No correspondence between perturbation, molecular mediator, and predeclared cell-state endpoint.
The effect disappears after line, batch, region, stress, or developmental-alignment controls.
A multiplex effect is no stronger than matched single-candidate and neutral-edit controls after multiplicity correction.
selected_primary_direction.claim_ceiling: Conditional causal support for a defined cortical developmental module; not a claim about cognition, language, consciousness, or complete human uniqueness.

research_conclusion: The most productive answer is likely modular rather than monogenic: human-specific cortical development may emerge from interacting duplicated-gene dosage, enhancer sequence, and three-dimensional regulatory changes. CortexSwitch makes that proposition testable by requiring reciprocal human reversion and chimpanzee humanization, independent lines, molecular mediation, and organoid-fidelity gates. If those conditions are met, the study would support a conditional human-lineage developmental module; if not, it would identify which apparent human-specific signals are background-, protocol-, or model-dependent.

required_review_topics: primate genomic and cellular material governance
organoid oversight and developmental model limits

known_scientific_risks: Candidate prioritization and gap interpretation remain dependent on published evidence and model-assisted synthesis.
Organoids may retain batch, maturation, regional-identity, and stress confounding.
Human-lineage sequence status and enhancer-to-target-gene assignment can remain uncertain.
Reciprocal perturbation cannot by itself establish organism-level human uniqueness.
